content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents a method for learning the connectivity pattern for Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM). By this we mean a sparsity map on the weight matrix of the model. The method works by reparameterizing the weight matrix as a product of continuous weights and binary masks. The binary masks are represented through a hard thresholding operation applied to a continuous strength parameter. A straight-through gradient estimator is used to learn this continuous strength parameter. The authors present experimental results on MNIST and two other benchmark datasets evaluating the models for classification accuracy and log-likelihood (with AIS). Empirical results demonstrate that the sparsely connected RBMs outperform their dense counterparts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The paper is clearly written and the method appears to function as the authors claim. While not particularly in depth, the emperical evaluation indicates that sparse conenctivity may be a useful inductive bias for these models and the proposed approach is simpler than alternative regularizations for RBMs such as hidden feature sparsity (https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2007/hash/c60d060b946d6dd6145dcbad5c4ccf6f-Abstract.html) for example. 

Weaknesses:

Overall I had some issues with this work. This optimization approach for learning binary parameters has been explored in many prior works (for example https://arxiv.org/pdf/1603.05279.pdf) and has seen successful adoption for many applications such as sparse bayesian models, binary nets, and more. Although this is, to my knowledge, the first application I've seen towards learning undirected models. 

I feel the work could have been improved with a more thorough dive into the types of connectivity patters the models were learning. Sparse connections are a useful inductive bias if there is truly a sparse covariance pattern in the training data. If we are recovering the true sparse connectivity that exists in the data, that would be quite interesting. As it stands, that is not clear. This could be demonstrated in an artificial data setting where such sparsely connected data is generated and then models are trained and we can examine if the correct pattern is recovered. 

I also feel that there are a number of obvious baseline methods for learning sparse networks which were not explored here. Why not run some comparisons to L1-regularized RBMs? This simple technique has been widely explored for learning Ising and Potts models and is the de-facto standard in protein applications for example. Besides this there are methods for sparse variational inference (such as https://arxiv.org/pdf/1602.03807.pdf) which were not mentioned. This prior work also addresses the bias in their gradient estimators which this work does not. 

Last, I do not see why this approach is restricted to RBMs. We could easily apply the same method to other connection based models like Ising and Potts models. There exist simple benchmarks like recovering ground truth sparsity patterns in sparse Ising models and protein contact prediction with Potts models.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clear, and well written and easy to follow. Overall though, I do not believe this method is particularly novel given that the same approach has been utilized in a number of other applications for a number of years. As well, there exist a number of more sophisticated methods for this application which have also been published years ago. 

I do believe that the paper's results are reproducible as the experimental details are clearly written and all hyper-parameters are specified.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents a method for learning sparse connectivity patterns in RBMs based on a straight-through gradient estimator. While the method appears to work as indicated, the method lacks novelty as more sophisticated approaches exist and the proposed approach has already been applied in a number of other applications.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an algorithm to learn the connectivity pattern of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM). The key idea is to parameterize the connectivity pattern and use a gradient-based update to automatically adjust this pattern. Empirically, the proposed method achieves better convergence and final performance on two tasks (sample generation and classification) on MNIST and UCI datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Most parts of the paper are clearly written and are well-motivated.
- The work is relevant to the ICLR community.

Weaknesses:
- The paper has limited novelty (see the comment below).
- Another concern lies in the evaluation setup. The authors fixed the parameter learning rate to $\alpha = 0.1$ and $\alpha = 0.01$ for MNIST and UCI experiments, respectively. Similarly, the connectivity learning rates are fixed to $\alpha_A = 0.5$ and $\alpha = 0.01$. However, the details of how these hyperparameters are selected are not described in the paper. It is likely that the optimal learning rates for the dense connectivity pattern and sparse connectivity pattern are different, but these are not taken into consideration. I am concerned that the dense baseline is not strong enough.
- Moreover, the authors do not compare NCG to strong baseline methods such as stochastic gating (e.g., [1]) or even L1 regularization. While these are designed for general neural networks, I believe that the extension to RBM is straightforward.
- I also have several concerns about the experiment results (which I will describe below in the additional question section).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Originality
- The advantage of sparse connection in RBM was previously discussed in [1]. 
- Methods for (joint) automatic connectivity pattern selection in neural networks were also extensively discussed (e.g., [2, 3]).
- The proposed method Network Connectivity Gradient (NCG) is an extension of these two methods and one of my concerns about the paper is the limited novelty.  

2. Clarity
- The paper is well-motivated and the detailed background on RBM is helpful.
- The description of NCG (in Section 4) is quite ambiguous compared to other sections. Providing the algorithm for NCG would be really helpful as NCG is composed of many components (e.g., joint update, initialization).
- Overall, most parts of the paper are clearly written. 

3. Reproducibility
- Although the code is not provided, I believe that the authors provided enough details to reproduce the experiments. However, the details on how hyperparameters are selected are not provided.

4. Additional Comments
- I don’t understand how Eqn. 5 corresponds to computing a gradient of every combination. Does it simply mean that it computes the gradient of all connectivity patterns (all elements in the matrix $\mathbf{A}$)? Given the description in the abstract, I initially understood it as computing each gradient of $2^{n^2}$ possible combinations (in a structured manner).
- I don’t understand the last paragraph in Section 5. I thought that the goal is to achieve better performance by introducing a sparse connectivity pattern. 
- I also don't understand how different initialization probability results in different connection ratios. Ideally, regardless of this initialization, shouldn't the algorithm converge to the fixed final connectivity pattern (that is optimal on the training objective)?
- From Figure 4 and Figure 6, it seems like the dense network achieves much higher NLL even at initialization. With the correct initialization method, shouldn't they have a similar NLL at the beginning of the training? How are initial parameters (not connectivity patterns) being initialized?
- What happens if you retrain from the final connectivity pattern learned by NCG? Does it have the same final performance?
 
5. Minor Comments
- In the abstract, “... RBMs based on the idea of network gradients (NCG) …” → “... RBMs based on the idea of network connectivity gradients (NCG) …”.
- In Figure 1, it would be helpful to describe $H$ and $X$ in the caption.
- In Figure 2, I found the connection notation $x_1 - h_2$ to be quite confusing at first. I feel like notations based on adjacency matrix $(x_1, h_2)$ would make it more clear.
- Figure 3 seems to be unnecessary. 


[1] Amanda C. N. de Oliveira and Daniel R. Figueiredo. Network connectivity and learning performance on Restricted Boltzmann Machines. In International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), 2022.

[2] Yamada, Y., Lindenbaum, O., Negahban, S., & Kluger, Y. (2020, November). Feature selection using stochastic gates. In International Conference on Machine Learning (pp. 10648-10659). PMLR.

[3] Zhou, A., Ma, Y., Zhu, J., Liu, J., Zhang, Z., Yuan, K., ... & Li, H. (2021). Learning n: m fine-grained structured sparse neural networks from scratch. arXiv preprint arXiv:2102.04010.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I would give a rating of 3. While the paper is technically sound and the proposed method achieves good results on these small datasets, I have concerns about the (1) novelty, (2) experiment set-up, and (3) empirical analysis and lack of competitive baseline.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This submission proposes a strategy to add and remove connections from RBMs over the course of training. The approach computes a gradient for a continuous connection strength parameter associated with each weight, and then thresholds these connection strengths to achieve sparsity. Compared to a standard RBM baseline as well as RBMs with fixed sparse connectivity patterns and a previously proposed method for learning sparse RBMs (sparse evolutionary training), the proposed method performs better in terms of NLL (evaluated using AIS) on MNIST. It also obtains marginally higher classification accuracy when trained as a classification model by concatenating the labels to the input.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The proposed technique for training sparse RBMs is intuitive, simple to implement, and clearly described.
- The submission provides evaluation results in standard settings used by past work to evaluate RBMs, including NLL and classification accuracy on MNIST.
- The proposed technique appears to improve substantially over a standard dense RBM on these benchmarks.
- The submission provides some interesting additional analysis that shows that the final sparsity depends on the initial sparsity.

Weaknesses:

- I am a bit concerned about the NLL values reported, which seem higher than what has been reported in past work. Côté & Larochelle (2016) reports an average NLL of 86.50 for a baseline RBM with 500 hidden units trained with 10 CD steps, which seems substantially lower than either the value of ~150 reported for the baseline RBM here or the value of ~100 obtained with the proposed technique. Could the authors comment on the discrepancy?
- Related to this concern, I would like to see evidence that the hyperparameters/training methods chosen are near-optimal for the baseline. As far as I can tell, the submission investigates only a single combination of hyperparameters for all models. If these hyperparameters are suboptimal, it could be that the proposed method improves over the baseline in this experimental setting but fails to improve in others where the baseline performs better. In particular, I can imagine further tuning of the learning rate, applying weight decay, decaying the learning rate, using an adaptive optimizer could all yield improvements. Cho et al. (2011) propose some further improvements to RBM training that, in my anecdotal experience, are also quite effective. I’d like to be convinced that the approach presented here provides improvements over a well-tuned setup.

Minor:

- RBMs are not exactly a mainstream machine learning technique these days and there are few or no real-world applications for them. It is important that people do research on unpopular techniques, but this paper would probably find a larger readership if it could motivate the importance of its techniques to a broader audience.
- I assume that the results in Section 5.1 all involve MNIST since the paper says that “the main data set used is MNIST,” but this should be explicitly spelled out.
- The title on OpenReview is missing the word “Boltzmann.” Also, the definite article is awkward. It would be more grammatical to pluralize Restricted Boltzmann Machines (“Optimizing Connectivity through Network Gradients for Restricted Boltzmann Machines”).

References:

Cho, K., Raiko, T., & Ihler, A. T. (2011). Enhanced gradient and adaptive learning rate for training restricted Boltzmann machines. In Proceedings of the 28th international conference on machine learning (ICML-11) (pp. 105-112).

Côté, M. A., & Larochelle, H. (2016). An infinite restricted Boltzmann machine. Neural computation, 28(7), 1265-1288.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is well-written and the methodology is easy to understand.

Quality: I have concerns regarding the thoroughness of the empirical evaluation, described above under "weaknesses." I believe that these flaws are important to address.

Novelty: To my knowledge, there is no previous work exploring the approach used by this work to encourage sparsity in RBMs. However, the proposed approach simply trains a continuous parameter for each weight and then thresholds it to determine whether the weight should be retained or not. The approach alone doesn't seem sufficiently innovative to motivate acceptance of the paper by itself. However, if the empirical evaluation can convincingly show that imposing sparsity consistently leads to nontrivially better RBMs, I believe that would be a sufficiently novel finding to merit acceptance.

Reproducibility: Sufficient details are provided to reproduce the experiments in the paper, and the authors note that they will make the code available upon acceptance.
content.summary_of_the_review: The experiments suggest that the proposed method leads to better models, but there is no compelling justification for why it should lead to better Boltzmann machines. The absence of strong motivation for the proposed method does not necessarily mean it is not interesting. However, the experimental results must compellingly demonstrate that the method yields meaningful improvements and can serve as a building block for future empirical or theoretical work. In its present state, I do not believe that the experimental results presented meet this bar, although I am open to revising my assessment in response to further comments and experimentation.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
